name: Métro 1
description: Brussels metro line 1 crosses the city from Gare de l’Ouest to Stockel, sharing its central corridor with line 5. It links the city centre and Gare Centrale with the European quarter around Schuman before continuing through the eastern suburbs of Woluwe.

name: Métro 2
description: Line 2 follows a loop around central Brussels between Simonis and Elisabeth, two parts of the same interchange. Sharing its route with line 6, it connects Gare du Midi with Louise, Arts-Loi and Rogier, providing links to the city’s other metro lines and mainline trains.

name: Métro 5
description: Brussels metro line 5 runs from Erasme in Anderlecht through the city centre to Herrmann-Debroux in Auderghem. Its central section is shared with line 1, serving Gare Centrale and the European quarter before the route turns southeast through Delta and the city’s outer neighbourhoods.

name: Métro 6
description: Line 6 links Roi Baudouin and the Heysel area in northern Brussels with the loop around the city centre. From Simonis it shares the route of line 2 to Elisabeth, serving Gare du Midi, Louise and Arts-Loi along the way.

name: Métro M2
description: Charleroi’s M2 connects Monument in Anderlues with the city centre and Gare Centrale, passing through Fontaine-l’Évêque and the western suburbs. During the city-loop works it also replaces M1, keeping the western branch connected to the main railway station.

name: Métro M3
description: M3 links Faubourg de Bruxelles in Gosselies with central Charleroi, serving neighbourhoods along the northern approach to the city. Its two directions use different stops in Gosselies before joining the shared metro corridor through Palais and Waterloo to Gare Centrale.

name: Métro M4
description: Charleroi’s M4 runs from Soleilmont through Gilly to the city centre, joining the other metro branches at Waterloo and Palais. During the city-loop works it terminates at Ouest, providing an eastern light rail connection into central Charleroi.

name: Kusttram
description: The Kusttram follows Belgium’s North Sea coast from De Panne to Knokke, linking seaside towns including Nieuwpoort, Oostende, De Haan and Blankenberge. Its 67 stops provide access to beaches and coastal neighbourhoods, with mainline rail connections at Oostende and Blankenberge for journeys inland.

name: Appenzeller Bahnen Trogen–Appenzell
description: S20 is one of the services across the Appenzell–St Gallen mountain railway corridor, linking the Trogen branch with Appenzell via the city streets of St Gallen. The route brings together an urban tramway section and a rural railway through the rolling Appenzell landscape.

name: Appenzeller Bahnen Trogen–Appenzell
description: S21 follows the Appenzell–St Gallen–Trogen through route, using the shared city section to connect two regional branches. Its longer stopping pattern serves villages and neighbourhoods along the way, making it an important everyday link as well as a gateway to Appenzell’s hills.

name: Appenzeller Bahnen Trogen–Teufen
description: This service uses the Trogen railway’s steep approach from St Gallen and continues across the connected network toward Teufen. It combines close-set urban stops with a climb into the Appenzell region, where the line serves small communities beyond the city.

name: Aare Seeland mobil Solothurn–Langenthal
description: Known locally as the Bipperlisi, S11 links the Solothurn region with the Oberaargau around Langenthal, via Oensingen. Its branches serve communities between the Jura foothills and the Aare valley, with convenient connections to the mainline network at Solothurn, Oensingen and Langenthal.

name: Aare Seeland mobil Langenthal–St. Urban
description: S12 is the short regional branch from Langenthal to St Urban Ziegelei, serving the rural edge of the Oberaargau. It continues beyond the main Solothurn–Langenthal corridor into the Luthern valley area, connecting smaller communities with trains and services at Langenthal.

name: Bremgarten-Dietikon-Bahn
description: The Bremgarten–Dietikon railway connects the Reuss valley with Zürich’s western rail network, running from Wohlen through Bremgarten to Dietikon. Its route combines a regional railway across the countryside with frequent commuter connections at both ends.

name: Biel–Täuffelen–Ins-Bahn
description: S37 follows the southern shore of Lake Biel between Biel/Bienne and Ins, passing through the Seeland’s lakeside villages and agricultural lowlands. The line provides local access to communities that sit away from the mainline railway and connects onward at both termini.

name: Bex–Villars–Bretaye
description: The Bex–Villars–Bretaye railway climbs from the Rhône valley through Gryon to the resort of Villars, then continues up to Col-de-Bretaye in the Alpine foothills. The route is especially valued for access to mountain walks and ski terrain, with wide views over the Chablais.

name: Ferrovia Lugano–Ponte Tresa
description: The Lugano–Ponte Tresa railway heads west from Lugano through the Malcantone region to the Italian border area. Its suburban stops serve communities around Lake Lugano, while the line also offers a relaxed rail approach to lakeside villages and the hills above the shore.

name: Forchbahn
description: The Forchbahn starts at Zürich Stadelhofen and runs through the city’s eastern suburbs before crossing open countryside to Esslingen. Opened in 1912, it has evolved from a rural railway into a commuter route while retaining its distinctive tram-like street section in Zürich.

name: Frauenfeld–Wil-Bahn
description: This narrow-gauge regional railway links Frauenfeld in the Thurgau with Wil in St Gallen, serving smaller towns and villages between the two centres. The line gives the region a direct cross-cantonal connection and meets the wider Swiss rail network at each end.

name: Métro m1
description: Lausanne’s m1 connects the Flon transport hub with Renens, passing through the university district and the campuses of UNIL and EPFL. The line serves students and local residents across western Lausanne, with interchanges to regional trains and the city’s other metro line.

name: Métro m2
description: The fully automated m2 descends from Croisettes on Lausanne’s northern hillside through the city centre to Ouchy on Lake Geneva. Its steep, north–south route ties residential districts to Lausanne-Flon, the main railway station and the waterfront in a single urban corridor.

name: Lausanne–Echallens–Bercher
description: The Lausanne–Echallens–Bercher railway runs from the underground Flon hub into the agricultural Gros-de-Vaud region. After crossing Lausanne’s northern suburbs, it serves Echallens and continues to Bercher, linking rural communities with the city’s metro and rail connections.

name: Limmattalbahn
description: Line 20 crosses the growing Limmat Valley from Zürich Altstetten through Schlieren and Dietikon to Killwangen-Spreitenbach. Opened in 2022, the 13.4-kilometre light rail line connects residential and employment areas with four S-Bahn stations along its route.

name: Littorail
description: Littorail runs from Place Pury in central Neuchâtel west along the shore of Lake Neuchâtel to Boudry. The line serves the lakeside suburbs and villages of the region, offering a scenic alternative to road travel between the city and the vineyards beyond.

name: RBS Bern–Solothurn
description: RE5 is the RegioExpress service between Bern and Solothurn, crossing the rural landscapes of the Bernese Mittelland. It links the two cantonal centres with a faster stopping pattern than local services and provides connections to regional and national trains at both ends.

name: RBS Bern–Worb Dorf
description: S7 runs from Bern’s central station to Worb Dorf, combining a city-centre tram-style segment with a suburban railway into the Worblen valley. It is a practical link for commuters and local trips, and shares parts of its route with Bern’s urban transport network.

name: RBS Bern–Bätterkinden
description: S8 links Bern with Bätterkinden, passing through the northern suburbs and the communities of the Limpach valley. The route provides a direct rail connection to the capital for towns that sit beyond the Bern S-Bahn’s busiest inner ring.

name: RBS Bern–Unterzollikofen
description: This short regional line connects Bern with Unterzollikofen, serving northern neighbourhoods and the communities along the Aare. Its compact route feeds into the city’s main rail hub, where passengers can transfer to national trains and the wider Bern S-Bahn network.

name: Waldenburgerbahn
description: The Waldenburg railway follows a narrow valley from Liestal to Waldenburg, serving villages at the foot of the Jura. Rebuilt and reopened in 2022 with modern metre-gauge trains, it preserves the valley’s local rail link while bringing the line up to contemporary standards.

name: Wynental- und Suhrentalbahn
description: Aarau is the junction for this Aargau light railway’s two branches: north through the Suhrental to Schöftland and south through the Wynental to Menziken. S14 connects towns in both valleys with the cantonal capital and onward mainline trains.

name: U-Bahn U1
description: Berlin’s U1 links Uhlandstraße with Warschauer Straße, passing the western shopping district before following the elevated railway through Kreuzberg. Wittenbergplatz, Gleisdreieck and Kottbusser Tor provide useful U-Bahn connections, while Warschauer Straße connects with the S-Bahn and tram network.

name: U-Bahn U2
description: The U2 crosses Berlin from Pankow to Ruhleben through Alexanderplatz, Potsdamer Platz and Zoologischer Garten. It connects several major shopping and cultural districts, with S-Bahn transfers at Schönhauser Allee, Alexanderplatz and Potsdamer Platz and western connections towards the Olympic Stadium area.

name: U-Bahn U3
description: The U3 runs from Krumme Lanke through Dahlem and Wilmersdorf to the elevated Kreuzberg corridor and Warschauer Straße. Dahlem-Dorf and Freie Universität serve the university district, while Wittenbergplatz and Nollendorfplatz connect with other western U-Bahn routes.

name: U-Bahn U4
description: Berlin’s short U4 stays within Schöneberg, linking Innsbrucker Platz with Nollendorfplatz through Rathaus Schöneberg and Bayerischer Platz. It provides local access to the district’s residential streets, with S-Bahn connections at Innsbrucker Platz and U7 transfers at Bayerischer Platz.

name: U-Bahn U5
description: The U5 connects Berlin Hauptbahnhof with Hönow through the government district, Museumsinsel, Alexanderplatz and the eastern residential boroughs. Brandenburger Tor, Lichtenberg and Wuhletal offer railway connections, making the line useful for both central sightseeing and journeys towards Hellersdorf.

name: U-Bahn U6
description: The U6 runs north–south through central Berlin between Kurt-Schumacher-Platz and Alt-Mariendorf in the currently stored service pattern. Friedrichstraße offers S-Bahn and regional connections, Unter den Linden connects with the U5, and Mehringdamm links with the U7. The northern extension to Alt-Tegel is closed for works.

name: U-Bahn U7
description: The U7 forms a long arc from Rudow through Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Wilmersdorf and Charlottenburg to Rathaus Spandau. It serves numerous local centres rather than Alexanderplatz, with useful railway connections at Neukölln, Jungfernheide and Spandau and U-Bahn transfers across the western network.

name: U-Bahn U8
description: The U8 connects Hermannstraße with Wittenau through Neukölln, Alexanderplatz, Gesundbrunnen and Reinickendorf. Its north–south route provides direct access to the Rosenthaler Platz area, while Hermannstraße, Jannowitzbrücke, Alexanderplatz, Gesundbrunnen and Wittenau connect with the S-Bahn.

name: U-Bahn U9
description: Berlin’s U9 links Rathaus Steglitz with Osloer Straße through Zoologischer Garten, Turmstraße and Leopoldplatz. It is a useful route between the southwest and northwest without crossing Alexanderplatz, with S-Bahn connections at Steglitz, Bundesplatz, Zoologischer Garten and Westhafen.

name: U-Bahn U1
description: Frankfurt’s U1 connects Ginnheim Mitte with Südbahnhof through Nordwestzentrum, Heddernheim and the central tunnel. It serves the Zeil shopping area at Hauptwache and crosses beneath the Main to Sachsenhausen, with railway connections at Hauptwache and Südbahnhof.

name: U-Bahn U2
description: The U2 links Ober-Eschbach with Frankfurt Südbahnhof through Nieder-Eschbach, Heddernheim and Hauptwache. It provides a direct route from northern suburbs into the city centre. During the Bad Homburg extension works, Ober-Eschbach is the rail terminus and Gonzenheim is reached by replacement bus.

name: U-Bahn U3
description: The U3 connects Oberursel Hohemark with Frankfurt Südbahnhof, combining a suburban surface route with the central U-Bahn tunnel. Oberursel Bahnhof provides an S-Bahn interchange, while Hohemark is a gateway to the Taunus. Central transfers include Hauptwache and Willy-Brandt-Platz.

name: U-Bahn U4
description: Frankfurt’s U4 runs from Bockenheimer Warte through Hauptbahnhof and the city centre to Enkheim. It serves the exhibition district at Festhalle/Messe, crosses the central shopping area at Konstablerwache and continues through Bornheim, with mainline connections at Hauptbahnhof.

name: U-Bahn U5
description: The U5 connects Frankfurt Hauptbahnhof with Preungesheim through Willy-Brandt-Platz, Konstablerwache and the northern city districts. It gives the Hauptfriedhof area a direct route to the main railway station. The proposed Europaviertel extension is separate from the currently stored route.

name: U-Bahn U6
description: Frankfurt’s U6 links Hausen with Ostbahnhof through Bockenheimer Warte, Hauptwache, Konstablerwache and Zoo. It connects the northwest with the eastern railway station, offering central transfers to the S-Bahn and other U-Bahn routes without passing through Frankfurt Hauptbahnhof.

name: U-Bahn U7
description: The U7 connects Heerstraße in western Frankfurt with Enkheim through Bockenheimer Warte, Hauptwache, Konstablerwache and Zoo. It serves both western residential districts and the eastern suburbs, with S-Bahn transfers in the city centre and connections to the U4 on the Enkheim corridor.

name: U-Bahn U8
description: Frankfurt’s U8 connects Riedberg with Südbahnhof through Heddernheim, Hauptwache and the central tunnel. It gives the Riedberg district a direct route to the city centre and Sachsenhausen, with connections to the U9 for journeys towards Ginnheim and Nieder-Eschbach.

name: U-Bahn U9
description: The U9 links Ginnheim Mitte with Nieder-Eschbach through Nordwestzentrum and Riedberg. It forms an outer connection across northern Frankfurt rather than entering the city-centre tunnel, providing transfers to the U1, U2, U3 and U8 for onward journeys towards central Frankfurt.

name: U-Bahn U1
description: Hamburg’s U1 connects Norderstedt Mitte with two northeastern branches ending at Ohlstedt and Großhansdorf. It passes through central Hamburg and serves important interchanges including Jungfernstieg, Hauptbahnhof Süd and Wandsbek Markt. Check the branch destination when travelling beyond Volksdorf.

name: U-Bahn U2
description: The U2 runs from Niendorf Nord through central Hamburg to Mümmelmannsberg. It serves Hagenbecks Tierpark, Schlump, Jungfernstieg and Hauptbahnhof Nord before continuing through the eastern districts. Jungfernstieg and the Hauptbahnhof provide useful connections to the S-Bahn and regional railway network.

name: U-Bahn U3
description: Hamburg’s U3 follows the inner-city ring and continues to Wandsbek-Gartenstadt via Barmbek. Its elevated waterfront section serves Landungsbrücken and Baumwall, while other stops connect St. Pauli, the central station and residential districts. Barmbek is an important interchange with the S-Bahn.

name: U-Bahn U4
description: The U4 connects Billstedt with Elbbrücken through central Hamburg and HafenCity. It shares the eastern corridor with the U2 before branching towards Überseequartier and HafenCity Universität. Elbbrücken provides an S-Bahn interchange; the planned Horner Geest extension is outside the current route.

name: U-Bahn U1
description: Munich’s U1 connects Olympia-Einkaufszentrum with Mangfallplatz through Rotkreuzplatz, Hauptbahnhof and Sendlinger Tor. It links the northwestern and southeastern districts while serving the main railway station, with additional U-Bahn connections at Olympia-Einkaufszentrum, Hauptbahnhof, Sendlinger Tor and Kolumbusplatz.

name: U-Bahn U2
description: The U2 crosses Munich from Feldmoching to Messestadt Ost through Hauptbahnhof and Sendlinger Tor. It serves the exhibition grounds at Messestadt West and East, with S-Bahn connections at Feldmoching, Hauptbahnhof, Giesing and Trudering and transfers across the central U-Bahn network.

name: U-Bahn U3
description: Munich’s U3 connects Moosach with Fürstenried West through Olympiazentrum, Münchner Freiheit, Marienplatz and Sendlinger Tor. It serves the Olympic Park area and central shopping district, while Moosach and Marienplatz offer S-Bahn connections for onward journeys across the region.

name: U-Bahn U4
description: The U4 links Arabellapark with Westendstraße through Max-Weber-Platz, Odeonsplatz and Munich Hauptbahnhof. It connects the northeastern districts with the city centre and the western shared corridor, providing transfers to the U5, other U-Bahn lines and mainline trains at the central station.

name: U-Bahn U5
description: Munich’s U5 connects Laimer Platz with Neuperlach Süd through Hauptbahnhof, Odeonsplatz and Ostbahnhof. It serves the eastern residential districts and provides several S-Bahn interchange options, including Heimeranplatz, Hauptbahnhof, Ostbahnhof and Neuperlach Süd. The future western extension is outside the stored route.

name: U-Bahn U6
description: The U6 links Garching-Forschungszentrum with Klinikum Großhadern through Fröttmaning, Münchner Freiheit and Marienplatz. It serves the Garching research campus, Allianz Arena access at Fröttmaning and central university areas, with S-Bahn transfers at Marienplatz and Harras and U-Bahn connections across the city.

name: U-Bahn U7
description: Munich’s supplementary U7 connects Olympia-Einkaufszentrum with Neuperlach Zentrum through Hauptbahnhof, Sendlinger Tor and Innsbrucker Ring. It joins parts of the U1, U2 and U5 corridors into a direct route, so passengers should check its operating times rather than assume the main lines’ service pattern.

name: U-Bahn U8
description: The U8 is a supplementary Munich route between Olympiazentrum and Neuperlach Zentrum through Scheidplatz, Hauptbahnhof and Sendlinger Tor. It connects the Olympic Park corridor directly with the southeastern districts by combining sections of other U-Bahn routes. Check the timetable for the days it operates.

name: U-Bahn U1
description: The U1 connects Fürth Hardhöhe with Nuremberg Langwasser Süd through both cities’ main railway stations. It serves Fürth Rathaus, Plärrer and central Nuremberg before reaching the exhibition grounds at Messe, making it useful for intercity connections, city-centre trips and trade-fair visits.

name: U-Bahn U2
description: Nuremberg’s U2 connects Röthenbach with Flughafen through Plärrer and Hauptbahnhof. It provides a direct airport link from the main railway station and serves Nordostbahnhof along the northern section. Central interchange stations connect with the U1 and the shared U3 corridor.

name: U-Bahn U3
description: The U3 connects Großreuth bei Schweinau with Nordwestring through Plärrer, Hauptbahnhof and Rathenauplatz. It shares the central tunnel with the U2 before branching towards the northern residential districts and Klinikum Nord. Planned extensions beyond Großreuth are outside the current route.

name: Metro M1
description: M1 connects Vanløse with Vestamager, crossing central Copenhagen before continuing south through Amager and the modern Ørestad district. Along the way it serves university, residential and business areas, with transfers to S-trains and the rest of the metro network.

name: Metro M2
description: M2 shares the central route from Vanløse before turning across Amager to Copenhagen Airport. It is the metro’s direct airport link, also serving residential districts and connecting the city centre with Kastrup and the eastern side of the island.

name: Cityringen
description: Cityringen is Copenhagen’s underground loop, circling the inner city and linking districts such as Frederiksberg, Nørrebro, Østerbro and Vesterbro. It opened in 2019 and brings metro access close to many neighbourhoods without requiring every trip to pass through one central interchange.

name: Metro M4
description: M4 connects the redeveloped harbour districts of Nordhavn and Sydhavn with central Copenhagen, sharing its central section with the Cityringen. The line serves major rail interchanges at Østerport and København H, helping connect new waterfront neighbourhoods to the wider city.

name: Metrolinja M1
description: M1 stretches from Kivenlahti in Espoo through central Helsinki to Vuosaari on the eastern coast. It combines the western metro extension with the city’s long-running east–west corridor, linking suburban centres, downtown and residential districts on both sides of the capital.

name: Metrolinja M2
description: M2 runs from Tapiola in Espoo through Helsinki’s centre to Mellunmäki in the east. Sharing much of its central alignment with M1, it provides a more direct connection for northeastern suburbs and links Tapiola’s commercial and cultural district with the metro network.

name: Luas Green Line
description: Dublin’s Luas Green Line links Broombridge with Brides Glen through Phibsborough, the city centre, Dundrum and Sandyford. Central stops differ by direction: northbound trams use Westmoreland and O’Connell Street, while southbound trams serve Parnell, Marlborough and Trinity. Broombridge provides a railway interchange, and the route passes St Stephen’s Green and Harcourt.

name: Luas Red Line
description: Dublin’s Luas Red Line connects Tallaght and Saggart with the city centre, Connolly station and The Point in the Docklands. It serves Heuston, the museum district and the Four Courts; branches at Belgard and near Busáras make the destination important, while Abbey Street offers a walking interchange with the Green Line.

name: Linea T1
description: Running from Bergamo station into the Seriana Valley, T1 links the city with a string of suburban communities including Torre Boldone, Ranica and Albino. Opened in 2009, it reuses part of the historic valley railway corridor and connects with regional trains at Bergamo FS.

name: Linea T2
description: Planned as an extension of Bergamo’s tram network, T2 will run west toward Villa d’Almè along the former Valle Brembana railway corridor. The 9.8-kilometre route through Ponteranica and Sorisole is designed to connect hillside neighbourhoods and valley towns with Bergamo’s rail hub.

name: Metropolitana di Brescia
description: This fully automated line crosses Brescia from the northern districts to Sant’Eufemia-Buffalora in the southeast, passing beneath the historic centre. Since opening in 2013, it has offered a high-capacity alternative to buses, with park-and-ride links at several outer stations.

name: Tram 1
description: The red route links central Cagliari’s Piazza Repubblica with the university and hospital campus at Policlinico, via Monserrato. It combines an urban tramway with a suburban rail corridor, giving passengers a direct connection between the city centre and a major regional destination.

name: Tram 2
description: From Monserrato, Line 2 runs northeast to Settimo San Pietro, extending the metro-tram network into the metropolitan hinterland. Its short, five-stop route shares the San Gottardo interchange with Line 1, where passengers can continue toward central Cagliari or the Policlinico campus.

name: Metropolitana di Catania
description: Catania’s metro grew from the urban section of the historic Ferrovia Circumetnea, whose first underground service began in 1999. Today the line crosses the city centre between Stesicoro and Monte Po, with the volcanic slopes of Mount Etna rising beyond its western terminus.

name: Metropolitana di Catanzaro
description: This unusual regional metro service links hilltop Catanzaro Città with Catanzaro Lido on the Ionian coast. The route includes the steep rack-railway section between the upper city and Catanzaro Sala, then continues through the isthmus toward the mainline railway interchange at the coast.

name: Circumvesuviana Napoli–Baiano
description: The inland Circumvesuviana corridor runs from Naples through Nola to Baiano, serving towns on the eastern side of Mount Vesuvius and continuing into Avellino province. A separate branch in the catalog reaches Acerra, reflecting the network’s role in connecting the wider metropolitan area.

name: Circumvesuviana Napoli–Poggiomarino
description: This route leaves Naples for the southern Vesuvian plain, passing through the Pompeii and Torre Annunziata area before reaching Poggiomarino. It is part of the historic Circumvesuviana network, built to link the growing towns around Vesuvius with the regional capital.

name: Circumvesuviana Napoli–San Giorgio
description: A short but distinctly urban branch, this service connects Naples with San Giorgio a Cremano through the eastern suburbs. Its alignment also serves the Centro Direzionale business district, bringing the Circumvesuviana into one of the city’s main employment and rail-interchange areas.

name: Circumvesuviana Napoli–Sarno
description: Heading southeast from Naples, the Sarno route crosses the Vesuvian towns and continues into the Agro Nocerino-Sarnese, serving communities in both the Naples and Salerno areas. It follows the inland side of the Circumvesuviana network rather than the better-known coastal route to Sorrento.

name: Circumvesuviana Napoli–Sorrento
description: The best-known Circumvesuviana journey follows the Bay of Naples toward Sorrento, stopping near major archaeological sites including Herculaneum and Pompeii. Beyond the urban fringe, the railway hugs the Sorrentine Peninsula and provides a frequent link for residents and visitors alike.

name: Ferrovia a cremagliera di Granarolo
description: Built in 1901, this compact rack railway climbs from beside Genova Principe station to the hillside neighbourhood of Granarolo. Its 1.1-kilometre track rises nearly 200 metres, making it both a practical link for residents and a distinctive piece of Genoa’s historic vertical transport network.

name: Metropolitana di Genova
description: Genoa’s single metro line runs from Brin in the Polcevera valley to Brignole, linking the port, historic centre and two major railway stations. The first section opened in 1990; the line’s compact route makes its interchanges with trains and buses especially important in the city’s steep terrain.

name: Metropolitana M1
description: Opened in 1964, Milan’s red line was the city’s first metro and helped shape its modern network. Its two western branches reach Rho Fiera and Bisceglie, while the shared central section serves major interchanges including Cadorna, Duomo and Loreto before continuing north to Sesto.

name: Metropolitana M2
description: The green line ties Milan’s central rail hubs to distant suburbs on three branches: Gessate and Cologno Nord to the northeast, and Assago to the southwest. It passes through Cadorna and Centrale, making it a key cross-city route for commuters and visitors.

name: Metropolitana M3
description: Milan’s yellow line cuts diagonally through the centre from San Donato in the southeast to Comasina in the north. It serves Duomo and Centrale, creating useful connections with the city’s other metro lines and with long-distance and regional trains.

name: Metropolitana M4
description: The blue line connects Linate Airport with San Cristoforo, crossing central Milan and meeting the wider rail network along the way. The airport-to-city-centre journey takes about 12 minutes, giving air travellers a direct rapid-transit link into the city.

name: Metropolitana M5
description: Milan’s lilac line is a fully automated metro linking the San Siro stadium district with the northern suburbs around Bicocca and Bignami. It connects with M1 at Lotto, M3 at Zara and M2 at Garibaldi, helping distribute event crowds as well as everyday journeys.

name: Linea 1
description: Naples’ Line 1 links the northern districts of Piscinola and Scampia with the historic centre and Centro Direzionale, crossing the hills of Vomero on the way. Its celebrated ‘Stations of the Art’ pair major interchanges with architecture, public artworks and archaeological discoveries.

name: Linea 6
description: Line 6 connects the western district of Fuorigrotta with central Piazza Municipio, bringing the exhibition area, stadium quarter and waterfront into the metro network. Its contemporary stations include substantial architectural and art installations, and it interchanges with Line 1 at Municipio.

name: Linea 11
description: This suburban metro runs from Piscinola through Mugnano and Giugliano to Aversa, crossing the northern Naples metropolitan area and reaching into Caserta province. At Piscinola it connects with Naples Metro Line 1, giving outlying communities a rail link to the city centre.

name: Pisa Mover
description: Pisa’s automated people mover provides a direct airport-to-railway-station connection, with an intermediate stop at San Giusto/Aurelia. The full ride takes about five minutes, making it a quick link between Galileo Galilei Airport, Pisa Centrale and the city’s regional and national train services.

name: Ferrovia del Renon
description: The Renon narrow-gauge railway has served the South Tyrolean plateau since 1907, when it formed part of a longer mountain journey from Bolzano. The surviving line runs between Maria Himmelfahrt and Collalbo through meadows and woodland, with views toward the Dolomites and historic railcars on selected trips.

name: Linea A
description: Rome’s orange line runs from Battistini in the northwest to Anagnina in the southeast, passing the Vatican area, Piazza di Spagna and Termini. Since opening in 1980, it has become a major cross-city route, connecting residential districts with central landmarks and the city’s main railway hub.

name: Linea B
description: Opened in 1955 as Rome’s first metro, Line B links Laurentina and the EUR district with Termini, the Colosseum area and the northeast suburbs. Beyond Bologna, trains serve either Rebibbia or Jonio, while interchanges at Piramide and Tiburtina connect the line to regional and national rail.

name: Linea C
description: Rome’s driverless Line C carries passengers from Monte Compatri-Pantano through the eastern suburbs to the Colosseum, joining the historic centre with neighbourhoods far beyond the ring road. Archaeological finds shaped the design of several stations, turning key stops into showcase ‘archaeo-stations’.

name: Metromare
description: The former Roma–Lido railway opened in 1924 to connect the capital with its seaside district; today Metromare runs from Piramide to Cristoforo Colombo in Ostia. Along the way it serves Ostia Antica’s archaeological site and provides an everyday commuter link between the coast and central Rome.

name: Metropolitana M1
description: Turin’s driverless metro runs west to southeast from Fermi to Bengasi, connecting Collegno and the city with the Lingotto district. The first section opened for the 2006 Winter Olympics, and the line’s VAL technology made it Italy’s first fully automated metro system.

name: Tram T1
description: Luxembourg’s T1 connects Findel Airport with Stadion, crossing the Kirchberg district and city centre before continuing through Bonnevoie and Howald. It serves Gare Centrale and Howald’s railway interchange; at Rout Bréck–Pafendall, the funicular provides a connection down to Pfaffenthal-Kirchberg station in the valley.

name: Metro 50
description: Amsterdam’s Ringlijn runs from Isolatorweg through Sloterdijk, Lelylaan and Zuid to Gein in the southeast. Its orbital route connects the western suburbs with the southern business district and Bijlmer ArenA, with transfers to mainline trains at several stations and to the Noord/Zuidlijn at Zuid.

name: Metro 51
description: Line 51 connects Amsterdam Centraal with Isolatorweg via Amstel, RAI and Zuid before following the western ring through Lelylaan and Sloterdijk. It links the historic centre with southern and western districts, sharing its central tunnel with lines 53 and 54 and much of the ring route with line 50.

name: Metro 52
description: The Noord/Zuidlijn connects Noord with Zuid beneath the IJ and central Amsterdam, serving Rokin, Vijzelgracht, De Pijp and Europaplein. Opened in 2018, line 52 links neighbourhoods on both sides of the water with the city centre and offers mainline rail connections at Centraal and Zuid.

name: Metro 53
description: Amsterdam’s line 53 runs from Centraal Station through Nieuwmarkt, Waterlooplein and Amstel to Gaasperplas in the southeast. Beyond Van der Madeweg it serves Venserpolder, Diemen Zuid and the eastern Bijlmer neighbourhoods around Ganzenhoef and Kraaiennest, with an interchange to mainline trains at Diemen Zuid.

name: Metro 54
description: Line 54 links Amsterdam Centraal with Gein via Amstel, Duivendrecht, Bijlmer ArenA and Holendrecht. It provides a direct route from the city centre to southeastern residential districts and the Johan Cruijff ArenA, which can be reached from either Strandvliet or Bijlmer ArenA station.

name: RandstadRail 3
description: RandstadRail 3 connects Loosduinen in western The Hague with Zoetermeer, passing through the city-centre tram tunnel and Den Haag Centraal. Beyond Leidschenveen it follows the Zoetermeer circuit, serving neighbourhoods around Centrum-West and calling at the separate Voorweg Laag and Voorweg Hoog stops.

name: RandstadRail 4
description: RandstadRail 4 runs from De Uithof through Leyenburg and central The Hague to Zoetermeer’s Oosterheem district and Lansingerland-Zoetermeer station. It serves HagaZiekenhuis near Leyenburg and connects with mainline trains at Den Haag Centraal, Laan van NOI and Lansingerland-Zoetermeer, linking residential areas with regional rail services.

name: RandstadRail 34
description: Line 34 links De Savornin Lohmanplein in The Hague with Lansingerland-Zoetermeer via Den Haag Centraal and Zoetermeer Centrum-West. It combines the western corridor shared with line 3 and the Oosterheem branch shared with line 4, giving these districts a direct regional light rail connection.

name: Metro A
description: Rotterdam’s line A links Binnenhof in Ommoord with Schiedam Centrum via Alexander, Kralingse Zoom and the city centre. It connects with mainline trains at Alexander, Blaak and Schiedam Centrum, while Beurs provides transfers to the north–south metro lines D and E.

name: Metro B
description: Line B crosses Rotterdam from Nesselande to Hoek van Holland Strand, continuing west through Schiedam, Vlaardingen and Maassluis. The route brings the North Sea beach directly onto the metro network, with the western terminus beside the shore and central interchanges at Blaak and Beurs.

name: Metro C
description: Line C connects De Akkers in Spijkenisse with De Terp in Capelle aan den IJssel via Hoogvliet, Pernis and Schiedam. Its central section serves Delfshaven, Beurs and Blaak, linking communities southwest and east of Rotterdam with the city centre and mainline trains at Schiedam Centrum.

name: Metro D
description: Rotterdam’s line D runs from Rotterdam Centraal to De Akkers in Spijkenisse via Beurs, Wilhelminaplein and Zuidplein. South of Slinge it continues through Rhoon, Poortugaal and Hoogvliet, connecting suburban communities with the central railway station and the regional bus interchange at Zuidplein.

name: Metro E
description: Metro E links Den Haag Centraal with Slinge via Pijnacker, Berkel en Rodenrijs and Rotterdam Centraal. At Beurs it connects with the east–west metro corridor; Meijersplein / Airport provides a bus connection to Rotterdam The Hague Airport, while the metro itself continues through Rotterdam’s centre and southern districts.

name: Bybanen linje 1
description: Bergen’s first light rail line runs from the city centre south through Nesttun and Rådal to Bergen Airport Flesland. Opened in stages from 2010 to 2017, it serves residential districts, shopping centres and the airport on a dedicated urban corridor.

name: Bybanen linje 2
description: Line 2 links Bergen’s centre with Fyllingsdalen via Haukeland University Hospital and Kronstad. Opened in 2022, it creates a useful cross-city connection for hospital staff and visitors, and includes a long tunnel beneath the hills south of the city centre.

name: Gråkallbanen
description: Trondheim’s Gråkallbanen tram climbs from Ila through the western suburbs to Lian, at the edge of Bymarka forest. The line offers an everyday connection for local neighbourhoods and a direct ride to walking trails, lakes and outdoor recreation in the hills above the city.

name: T-bane 1
description: Line 1 is Oslo’s scenic Holmenkollen route, running from the southeastern suburbs through the city and up into the hills to Frognerseteren. It passes the ski-jump area at Holmenkollen and continues to forest trails and viewpoints, making it both a commuter line and an outdoor gateway.

name: T-bane 2
description: Line 2 crosses Oslo from Ellingsrudåsen in the east to Østerås in the west, passing through the city-centre tunnel. It connects outer residential districts with central stations and links to rail, tram and other metro lines along the way.

name: T-bane 3
description: Line 3 spans Oslo’s west and southeast, joining Kolsås with Mortensrud through the central metro network. It serves established suburban corridors at both ends and provides a direct ride across the city for commuters travelling between Bærum, downtown and the southern districts.

name: T-bane 4
description: Line 4 links Bergkrystallen in Oslo’s southeast with Vestli in the northeast, crossing the centre and serving many of the city’s eastern residential areas. Its route connects major interchange stations with neighbourhoods that rely on the metro for everyday trips into town.

name: T-bane 5
description: Line 5 serves Oslo’s northern suburbs, with branches toward Sognsvann and Vestli connected through the central tunnel. It links university and recreation areas around Sognsvann with Groruddalen neighbourhoods, while its shared central section makes transfers across the metro network straightforward.

name: Linia metra M1
description: Warsaw’s first metro line runs north–south between Młociny and Kabaty, crossing the Vistula and passing through the city centre. Opened in stages between 1995 and 2008, it connects residential districts with central business areas and key rail interchanges.

name: Linia metra M2
description: M2 crosses Warsaw east–west from Bródno through the city centre to Bemowo, including a central crossing beneath the Vistula. Its stations connect major residential districts on both sides of the river and provide transfers to M1 and the city’s rail network.

name: Nockebybanan
description: Nockebybanan, numbered 12, is a short light rail line from Alvik to Nockeby through the residential neighbourhoods of western Stockholm. It serves areas such as Smedslätten and Ålsten, with connections to the Green metro line and Tvärbanan at Alvik.

name: Lidingöbanan
description: Lidingöbanan connects Ropsten with Gåshaga brygga across the southern part of Lidingö island. Numbered 21, the line serves the island’s residential neighbourhoods and waterfront areas, linking them with Stockholm’s Red metro line at Ropsten.

name: Saltsjöbanan 25
description: Saltsjöbanan 25 connects Saltsjö-Järla with Saltsjöbaden through Nacka’s residential districts, including Saltsjö-Duvnäs and Fisksätra. Igelboda is the interchange for the Solsidan branch, line 26. During the western section’s reconstruction, replacement buses provide onward travel toward Slussen; trains do not currently serve the line’s original city terminus.

name: Saltsjöbanan 26
description: Line 26 is Saltsjöbanan’s short branch from Igelboda to Solsidan, serving Tippen, Tattby and Erstaviksbadet along the way. At Igelboda, passengers change to line 25 for Saltsjöbaden or Saltsjö-Järla, making the branch a local feeder for the wider Nacka rail corridor.

name: Roslagsbanan 27
description: Roslagsbanan 27 runs from Stockholms östra through Täby kyrkby and Vallentuna to Kårsta, serving suburban centres and smaller communities farther north. The route connects with the Red metro line at Tekniska högskolan beside its Stockholm terminus; the 27S express pattern skips selected intermediate stops.

name: Roslagsbanan 28
description: Line 28 connects Stockholms östra with Österskär via Täby centrum, Arninge and Åkersberga, serving the northeastern suburbs along Roslagsbanan’s eastern branch. It shares the inner corridor with the other Roslagsbanan lines before diverging at Roslags Näsby, and includes a 28S express pattern with fewer intermediate stops.

name: Roslagsbanan 29
description: Roslagsbanan 29 links Stockholms östra with Näsbypark, branching from the shared corridor at Djursholms Ösby to serve neighbourhoods including Altorp and Lahäll. It is the Roslagsbanan route serving Stocksund, with a connection to Stockholm’s Red metro line at Tekniska högskolan beside Stockholms östra.

name: Tvärbanan 30
description: Tvärbanan line 30 arcs around Stockholm’s inner suburbs from Sickla to Solna station, passing through Gullmarsplan, Årstaberg, Liljeholmen, Alvik and Sundbyberg. It connects several metro and commuter rail corridors, allowing journeys between neighbourhoods without passing through the city centre.

name: Tvärbanan 31
description: Tvärbanan line 31 links Alviks strand with Bromma flygplats, sharing the main Tvärbanan route as far as Norra Ulvsunda before branching toward Bromma Blocks. At Alvik it connects with the Green metro line and Nockebybanan, bringing the Bromma branch into Stockholm’s wider rail network.

name: Blå linjen
description: Stockholm’s Blue metro line brings routes 10 and 11 from Hjulsta and Akalla together at Västra skogen, continuing through Fridhemsplan and T-Centralen to Kungsträdgården. Its two branches connect the northwestern suburbs, including Sundbyberg, Solna and Kista, with the city centre.

name: Gröna linjen
description: Stockholm’s Green metro line links the western suburbs around Hässelby strand with three southern branches to Skarpnäck, Farsta strand and Hagsätra, numbered 17, 18 and 19. The shared corridor passes through Alvik, Odenplan, T-Centralen, Gamla stan and Södermalm before the branches separate south of Gullmarsplan.

name: Röda linjen
description: Stockholm’s Red metro line combines route 13 between Norsborg and Ropsten with route 14 between Fruängen and Mörby centrum. The routes share the central corridor through Liljeholmen, Södermalm, Gamla stan and T-Centralen, connecting southwestern suburbs with the northeastern side of the city.

name: Blackpool Tramway
description: Blackpool’s tramway follows the Fylde coast between Starr Gate and Fleetwood Ferry through the seafront, Bispham and Cleveleys. The route serves Blackpool’s piers and Pleasure Beach, while some journeys detour to North Station for mainline trains; direct coastal and North Station stopping patterns are both included.

name: Glasgow Subway
description: Glasgow’s Subway is a circular railway linking the city centre, West End and neighbourhoods south of the Clyde. Its fifteen stations include Buchanan Street, St Enoch, Hillhead, Partick and Govan; Inner and Outer Circle trains travel in opposite directions, with mainline railway connections at Partick and near Buchanan Street.

name: Bakerloo line
description: The Bakerloo line runs from Harrow & Wealdstone to Elephant & Castle, linking northwest London with the West End and the south bank of the Thames. It serves Paddington, Marylebone, Oxford Circus and Waterloo, making it useful for connections between mainline railway stations and central shopping and entertainment areas.

name: Central line
description: London’s Central line crosses the city from Ealing Broadway and West Ruislip to Epping and Hainault, passing through Oxford Circus, Bank and Stratford. Its eastern branches serve the Essex suburbs, with routes to Hainault approaching through either Newbury Park or the loop from Woodford.

name: Circle line
description: The Circle line connects Hammersmith with Edgware Road via a circuit around central London, serving Paddington, King’s Cross St Pancras, Liverpool Street, Victoria and Westminster. Its route includes both a western approach and the central loop, so Edgware Road appears twice on a complete journey through the line.

name: District line
description: The District line links Upminster in east London with western branches toward Ealing Broadway, Richmond and Wimbledon, alongside services through Edgware Road and Kensington Olympia. Its shared central corridor follows the north side of the Thames through Tower Hill, Embankment and Westminster before reaching Earl’s Court, a key branch interchange.

name: Docklands Light Railway
description: The Docklands Light Railway connects Bank and Tower Gateway with east and southeast London through Docklands. Its branches serve Canary Wharf, Greenwich, Lewisham, Beckton, Woolwich Arsenal and Stratford, including a stop at London City Airport; check the destination because trains share central sections before taking different branches.

name: Hammersmith & City line
description: The Hammersmith & City line runs from Hammersmith to Barking across the northern side of central London, calling at Paddington, King’s Cross St Pancras and Liverpool Street. It shares much of its route with the Circle line before continuing through Whitechapel, Mile End and the East End.

name: Jubilee line
description: London’s Jubilee line connects Stanmore with Stratford through Baker Street, Westminster, Waterloo and London Bridge. Its eastern section serves Canary Wharf, North Greenwich and Canning Town, linking the West End and major railway stations with Docklands and providing interchanges with the DLR and other Underground lines.

name: Metropolitan line
description: The Metropolitan line reaches from Aldgate into northwest London and the towns of Amersham, Chesham, Watford and Uxbridge. Baker Street and Harrow-on-the-Hill are important junctions along the route, which combines a central urban corridor with longer suburban journeys and distinct fast and stopping patterns.

name: Northern line
description: The Northern line connects Edgware, High Barnet and Mill Hill East with southern branches to Morden and Battersea Power Station. Two central routes run via Bank or Charing Cross, serving different interchanges; Camden Town and Kennington are key junctions when choosing a branch or changing trains.

name: Piccadilly line
description: The Piccadilly line links Cockfosters with Heathrow Airport and Uxbridge through King’s Cross St Pancras, the West End and South Kensington. At Heathrow, Terminal 4 services use a one-direction loop through Terminals 2 & 3, while a separate branch serves Terminal 5, making the train’s destination important for airport journeys.

name: Victoria line
description: London’s Victoria line runs from Walthamstow Central to Brixton, linking northeast and south London through the West End. It connects major railway interchanges at Tottenham Hale, King’s Cross St Pancras, Euston, Victoria and Vauxhall, with Oxford Circus providing access to the central shopping district and other Underground lines.

name: Waterloo & City line
description: The Waterloo & City line is a two-station Underground connection beneath the Thames between Waterloo and Bank. It links the mainline railway terminus on the South Bank with the City of London, where passengers can continue onto other Underground lines and the Docklands Light Railway.

name: Luton DART
description: Luton DART is the automated shuttle between Luton Airport Parkway railway station and the airport terminal. Its dedicated guideway climbs from the rail corridor to the airport, connecting passengers with Thameslink and East Midlands Railway services at Parkway and providing a direct alternative to a road transfer.

name: Metrolink Manchester Airport–Victoria
description: This Metrolink route connects Manchester Airport with Victoria via Wythenshawe, Sale Water Park and the city centre. It serves residential communities south of Manchester before joining the shared tram corridor at St Werburgh’s Road, with city-centre stops at Deansgate-Castlefield, St Peter’s Square, Market Street and Shudehill.

name: Metrolink Altrincham–Bury
description: The Altrincham–Bury service crosses Greater Manchester through Sale, Stretford, the city centre and Prestwich. It serves both Deansgate-Castlefield and Victoria, with further railway connections at Navigation Road and Altrincham; the central section runs via Market Street and Shudehill, linking the network’s northern and southwestern corridors.

name: Metrolink Altrincham–Etihad Campus
description: This Metrolink service links Altrincham with Etihad Campus via Sale, Old Trafford and central Manchester. It calls at Piccadilly before continuing through New Islington and Holt Town, providing a direct connection between the southwestern suburbs, the main railway station and the stadium district around Etihad Campus.

name: Metrolink Bury–Ashton-under-Lyne
description: The Bury–Ashton-under-Lyne service crosses Manchester via Prestwich, Victoria and Piccadilly before continuing past Etihad Campus toward Droylsden and Ashton. Its route joins northern and eastern suburbs through the city centre, with railway interchanges at Victoria and Piccadilly and bus connections at the outer termini.

name: Metrolink East Didsbury–Rochdale Town Centre
description: This cross-city Metrolink route links East Didsbury with Rochdale Town Centre through Chorlton, central Manchester and Oldham. It uses the city-centre crossing via Exchange Square and Victoria, then follows the northeastern corridor through Shaw and Crompton, with a railway interchange at Rochdale before reaching the town centre.

name: Metrolink East Didsbury–Shaw and Crompton
description: The East Didsbury–Shaw and Crompton service connects south Manchester with the Oldham corridor, passing through Chorlton, Exchange Square and Victoria. It serves the same intermediate stops as the longer Rochdale service up to Shaw and Crompton, providing an additional direct connection between these suburban areas and the city centre.

name: Metrolink MediaCityUK–Piccadilly
description: This Metrolink service links MediaCityUK and Salford Quays with Piccadilly railway station, passing through Exchange Quay, Cornbrook and Deansgate-Castlefield. It provides direct access from the waterfront district to central Manchester, with St Peter’s Square and Piccadilly Gardens offering onward connections across the tram and bus networks.

name: Metrolink Piccadilly–Eccles
description: The Piccadilly–Eccles service runs through central Manchester and Salford Quays before continuing through Langworthy, Weaste and Ladywell. Some journeys call at MediaCityUK, giving the line two distinct stopping patterns; Cornbrook is an important interchange for the Altrincham, airport, East Didsbury and Trafford Centre corridors.

name: Metrolink The Trafford Centre–Crumpsall
description: This Metrolink route connects The Trafford Centre with Crumpsall through Trafford Park, Salford Quays and central Manchester. It serves Trafford Palazzo, the Imperial War Museum and Wharfside before joining the shared route at Cornbrook, then continues via Exchange Square and Victoria to the northern suburbs.

name: Tram Train
description: The Tram Train connects Sheffield Cathedral with Rotherham Parkgate, sharing the city tram corridor before joining the railway beyond Meadowhall South / Tinsley. It serves the arena district, Magna and Rotherham Central, combining street-running access to central Sheffield with a regional rail connection into Rotherham.

name: Green line
description: The Green line connects Newcastle Airport with South Hylton via central Newcastle, Gateshead and Sunderland. It shares the central Metro corridor with the Yellow line and serves railway interchanges at Central Station, Heworth and Sunderland, linking the airport and surrounding residential communities with the wider regional network.

name: Yellow line
description: Tyne and Wear Metro’s Yellow line runs from St James around the North Tyneside coast through Tynemouth and Whitley Bay before returning through Newcastle and continuing to South Shields. Its horseshoe-shaped route visits Monument twice on different levels, connecting coastal towns with central Newcastle, Gateshead and South Tyneside.

name: West Midlands Metro
description: West Midlands Metro links Birmingham’s Edgbaston Village with Wolverhampton via the Jewellery Quarter, West Bromwich, Wednesbury and Bilston. It serves both Wolverhampton termini and Grand Central beside Birmingham New Street; some Birmingham-bound journeys turn back at Millennium Point, visiting Albert Street twice before continuing through the city centre.
